The reference engine model was based on the Trent 1000-R3 engine, which incorporates the latest technology upgrade and is certified for the highest static thrust.
The reference aircraft model was similar to the Boeing 787-8, with a maximum range of 13,841 km and a payload of 24,684 kg.
The thermodynamic cycle design considered operating conditions of cruise, maximum take-off on a hot day, and top of climb.
The maximum temperatures were constrained to 989 K at the high pressure compressor outlet, 1932 K at the high pressure turbine inlet, and 1270 K at the low pressure turbine inlet.
The cooling air extraction locations and split between working and non-working cooling air were kept constant across all engine designs.
The engine geometry was estimated using a knowledge-based process that relied on dimensionless geometric parameters extracted from a general arrangement drawing similar to the Trent 1000.
The reference engine model showed good agreement with available data on the Trent 1000 for parameters like bypass ratio, overall pressure ratio, and thrust specific fuel consumption.
The model parameters selected for the rubber engine model included the required thrust at sizing operating conditions, the design flight Mach number, and the engine diameter.

The use of surrogate models enabled the transformation of discrete transitions of integer-numbered parameters into continuous problems, facilitating multi-fidelity approaches and the determination of derivatives and sensitivities.

The hybrid surrogate-based rubber engine model combines surrogate models for engine parameters with a thermodynamic performance tool to enable evaluation of engine performance over the entire flight mission.
The proposed rubber engine model aims to simplify the MDO process by encapsulating the complex engine design as a preprocessing step, reducing complexity and increasing robustness.
The authors used the German Aerospace Center's (DLR) Gas Turbine Laboratory (GTlab) and DLR Performance Program (DLRp2) tools for engine design and thermodynamic cycle calculations.
The authors assessed different design of experiment and interpolation methods with varying numbers of samples to determine the most efficient way to build the rubber engine model.
The presented work was created in the context of the DLR's VicToria (Virtual Aircraft Technology Integration Platform) project.
The hybrid surrogate-based rubber engine model facilitates the exchange with other organizations or departments, as only common tools for meta-modeling and thermodynamic calculation are required.
